sm: The host introduces his guest, James Holland, described as a market analyst, and says the conversation will cover politics, the economy and how the war has affected both. Holland says the show is about how decisions in Washington reach gas pumps and grocery stores. Asked why Republicans lost in November, he says polling showed a significant group of Republican-leaning voters, perhaps twelve to fifteen million who routinely switch, flipped to Democrats, and that a rise in independents pulled away more Republican votes. He estimates about a quarter of those voters flopped out of emotion and three quarters flipped while looking for moral alignment. He says the Iran conflict mattered because the party had run on no new wars and America first, and voters paying high gas prices saw no justification.

The host says he sees the war as only about twenty percent of the problem, with the economics, such as high gas prices, as the other eighty. Holland adds that the Ukraine war, with estimates of 450,000 Russian and 250,000 to 350,000 Ukrainian dead, and attacks on energy infrastructure had already put the energy market on a simmer before Iran. He cites a post by Vice President Vance framing the war as either important enough to cost the Senate or overblown. He says enemies such as the Houthis can hit energy infrastructure and move prices, and that Venezuelan tankers seized by the US make little difference. On domestic oil, he says US refining runs at ninety-eight percent capacity, and adding more would take at least ten years.

Holland says leasing of drilling rights to other nations held back US refining, so the country is about eight years behind, and allies like Brazil offer limited capacity. The host gives his own view that the economy has long been a mix of government and business, with healthcare and education prices rising enormously since the 1970s. He argues that COVID shutdowns, supply chain breaks and stimulus created inflation of roughly eighteen percent through 2024. He says Trump's tariffs added about five percent more. He supports tariffs as a tool against Chinese slave labor but says they hurt businesses trading with Italy and Mexico, and that no one honestly explained the self-inflicted inflation.

The host says Trump keeps calling the economy great while people struggle, and mentions his local school levy raising his property taxes. Holland says Iran is only the last name in the credits, since the tariff war was never finished before a physical conflict began. He notes that allies like the UK could not have helped even if they wanted to, because they lack ships, planes and troops. He says rising diesel prices pushed up everything, and that gas had stayed manageable earlier in the year. He suspects Iran priorities came from cabinet members and longtime Washington figures such as Lindsey Graham, who assured Trump there would be no electoral cost, when young voters could have told him otherwise.

They turn to interest rates and the stock market. Holland says rates reflect that real inflation is more like fifteen to thirty percent, and that people who got raises should check their real earnings since 2019. He says the odds of a December rate hike rose from under fifty percent in July to over ninety percent, and that quarter or half point hikes could continue next year. He says housing is out of reach, with young men expecting to afford a home at thirty-five. They then discuss the Texas race and James Talarico. Holland says Talarico claimed taxing the top one percent could bring in 174 billion dollars, while he says interest on healthcare spending alone is about 186 billion.

Holland says the health care figure shows nobody has looked at how money is spent, and credits the Doge effort with being the first real attempt at cutting. The conversation moves to Nvidia, whose stock is around 160 dollars after its chief executive resigned amid moral scandals. Holland says it is either one of the best buys now or a sign the tech bubble is bursting. He notes that data center projects are being delayed, but says that could raise AI prices and margins. He says people expect Nvidia to reach 210 next year, and that whether data centers and AI demand are real will decide it. He adds that Elon Musk would call Tesla overvalued, yet it keeps rising.

Holland says that if Nvidia reaches 210 to 220 next year, buying at 160 will look excellent, and he thinks that more likely than AI and data centers being a ruse. Asked about 2027 with Democrats controlling Congress, he expects a stalemate, with possible action on healthcare, tech and consumer prices, and perhaps solar tax credits but not EV credits. He notes Vance was moved to domestic issues and Microsoft was pressed over H-1B visas, which he calls good traction. He says Trump should admit mistakes and finish three priorities. He expects oil traders to follow missile news, and healthcare premiums to rise, adding to inflation, and compares his own six to eight thousand dollar family deductible with the old plans.
